title: Song of Solomon 6:4–13
context: In the WEB headings, the Lover praises the beloved again, repeating images from 4:1–3 and setting her above queens and concubines (6:4–12); the Friends call the Shulammite to return, and the Lover replies (6:13). The sense of 6:12 is uncertain, as are the meanings of “Shulammite” and “the dance of Mahanaim.” Versification: English/WEB 6:13 is Hebrew 7:1, and 7:1–13 is Hebrew 7:2–14; this page keeps the WEB numbering, with 6:13 in chapter 6.

verses.text: You are beautiful, my love, as Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army with banners.
verses.arminianNotes: The WEB heading marks the Lover: “You are beautiful, my love, as Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army with banners.” Arminian readers see beauty joined with dignity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see majesty in the praise. Tirzah was a royal city of the northern kingdom in 1 Kings 16:23, though readers in this tradition hold its significance here with caution.

verses.text: Turn away your eyes from me, for they have overcome me. Your hair is like a flock of goats, that lie along the side of Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes: “Turn away your eyes from me, for they have overcome me.” The praise repeats images from 4:1. Arminian readers see the lover overwhelmed by the beloved’s presence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see deep admiration. The repetition of earlier imagery suggests renewed affection after the separation of chapter 5, whether read literally or allegorically.

verses.text: Your teeth are like a flock of ewes, which have come up from the washing, of which every one has twins; not one is bereaved among them.
verses.arminianNotes: “Your teeth are like a flock of ewes.” The praise repeats 4:2 with slight variation. Arminian readers see familiar images reaffirming love after the earlier distance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reuse of imagery as reaffirmation. Readers in this tradition caution against forcing symbolic meaning onto each pastoral detail.

verses.text: Your temples are like a piece of a pomegranate behind your veil.
verses.arminianNotes: “Your temples are like a piece of a pomegranate behind your veil.” Arminian readers see the earlier praise of 4:3 repeated, emphasizing steady affection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see continuity in the lover’s regard. The repeated line shows that the love expressed before the separation remains unchanged.

verses.text: There are sixty queens, eighty concubines, and virgins without number.
verses.arminianNotes: “There are sixty queens, eighty concubines, and virgins without number.” Arminian readers see the beloved set apart from a great crowd of others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a contrast emphasizing her uniqueness. The verse describes a royal setting without endorsing it, and readers in this tradition do not draw conclusions about marriage practices from it.

verses.text: My dove, my perfect one, is unique. She is her mother’s only daughter. She is the favorite one of her who bore her. The daughters saw her, and called her blessed. The queens and the concubines saw her, and they praised her.
verses.arminianNotes: “My dove, my perfect one, is unique.” Even queens and concubines praise her. Arminian readers see singular devotion that sets the beloved above all others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see her uniqueness affirmed. Allegorical readers often apply this to the church as one beloved people, while literal readers see exclusive love in marriage.

verses.text: Who is she who looks out as the morning, beautiful as the moon, clear as the sun, and awesome as an army with banners?
verses.arminianNotes: “Who is she who looks out as the morning, beautiful as the moon, clear as the sun, and awesome as an army with banners?” Arminian readers see radiance and majesty combined.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see splendid imagery. Allegorical readers have applied the verse to the church’s glory, while literal readers hear admiration of the beloved; readers in this tradition hold both approaches.

verses.text: I went down into the nut tree grove, to see the green plants of the valley, to see whether the vine budded, and the pomegranates were in flower.
verses.arminianNotes: “I went down into the nut tree grove, to see … whether the vine budded.” Arminian readers see springtime growth and anticipation pictured in the garden.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see images of new life. The speaker is debated, and readers in this tradition hold the WEB heading assigning these lines to the Lover as one reasonable reading.

verses.text: Without realizing it, my desire set me with my royal people’s chariots.
verses.arminianNotes: “Without realizing it, my desire set me with my royal people’s chariots.” Arminian readers note that this line is notoriously difficult and its meaning uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the obscurity of the verse. Translations render it in various ways, and readers in this tradition avoid building conclusions on a line whose sense is unclear.

verses.text: Return, return, Shulammite! Return, return, that we may gaze at you. Why do you desire to gaze at the Shulammite, as at the dance of Mahanaim?
verses.arminianNotes: The WEB headings give the Friends’ call, “Return, return, Shulammite!” and the Lover’s reply about the dance of Mahanaim. Arminian readers see others longing to see her.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the beloved’s beauty drawing attention. The meaning of “Shulammite” and “the dance of Mahanaim” is uncertain, and readers in this tradition hold proposed explanations loosely.
